Q: When it is best to apply Unique constraint? A:

A UNIQUE constraint depends on the business rules, not on the one-to-many relationship.

Usually, the subcategory name should be unique only inside its category: Example.

UNIQUE (category_id, english_name)

This prevents duplicate subcategories in the same category but allows the same name in different categories.

Use UNIQUE (english_name) only if the name must be unique across all categories.

Q: How to select last N observation from each group in dplyr dataframe? A:

Another base R ave() solution:

df[ave(seq_len(nrow(df)), df$a, FUN = \(i) last_n(i, 2L)), ]

last_n <- \(x, n) {
  stopifnot(n >= 1L)
  if (length(x) <= n) return(x) # could be less than n rows
  to_remove <- seq_len(length(x) - n)
  x[to_remove] <- 0L
  x
}

Q: Why the time complexity of pre-order is O(n) while print the nth node is O(2^n)? A:

The answer is that n has a different meaning in the two examples.

In the preOrder example, n is the number of nodes in the tree1. You are visiting all n nodes.

In the nthLevel example2, n is the level of the tree that you want to list. There will be up to 2^n nodes at level n of a binary tree. (The algorithm will visit a further up to 2^n nodes in reaching the level n nodes ... but that doesn't alter the complexity.)

1 - That should be explained in the textbook (or whatever) where you found the complexity analysis.
2 - In fact the nthLevel code you presented will fail if the tree is shallower than n or if it is not fully populated.

Q: OpenGL Trying to render a cube but there are weird lines between planes A:

Both the near plane and the far plane have to be positive values for glm::perspective and static_cast<float>(framebuffer_width / framebuffer_height) would be an integral division:

float fov = 90.f;
float nearPlane = 0.1f; // 0.1 instead of -1.0
float farPlane = 1000.f;

glm::mat4 ProjectionMatrix(1.f);
ProjectionMatrix = glm::perspective(glm::radians(fov), 
    static_cast<float>(framebuffer_width) / static_cast<float>(framebuffer_height),
    nearPlane, farPlane);

See glm::perspective:

GLM_FUNC_DECL mat<4, 4, T, defaultp> glm::perspective(
      T     fovy,
      T     aspect,
      T     near,
      T     far 
  )

[...]
near Specifies the distance from the viewer to the near clipping plane (always positive).
far Specifies the distance from the viewer to the far clipping plane (always positive).

The glm library provides matrix operations related to OpenGL and GLSL. The glm API documentation refers to The OpenGL Shading Language specification 4.20.

See The OpenGL Shading Language 4.6, 5.4.2 Vector and Matrix Constructors, page 101:

To initialize a matrix by specifying vectors or scalars, the components are assigned to the matrix elements in column-major order.

mat4(float, float, float, float,  // first column
       float, float, float, float,  // second column
       float, float, float, float,  // third column
       float, float, float, float); // fourth column

This means the transformation of the vertex coordinate in the vertex shader has to be: 

gl_Position = ProjectionMatrix * ViewMatrix * ModelMatrix * vec4(vertex_position,1.0);

See also GLSL Programming/Vector and Matrix Operations:

Likely the matrix can be transposed when set to the uniform, by setting the 3rd paramter of glUniformMatrix4fv to GL_TRUE: 

GLuint s = glGetUniformLocation(programID, "ModelMatrix");
glUniformMatrix4fv(s, 1, GL_TRUE, glm::value_ptr(ModelMatrix));

s = glGetUniformLocation(programID, "ProjectionMatrix");
glUniformMatrix4fv(s, 1, GL_TRUE, glm::value_ptr(ProjectionMatrix));

s = glGetUniformLocation(programID, "ViewMatrix");
glUniformMatrix4fv(s, 1, GL_TRUE, glm::value_ptr(ViewMatrix));

And compute the vertex coordinate transformation in the reverse order: 

gl_Position = vec4(vertex_position,1.0) * ModelMatrix * ViewMatrix * ProjectionMatrix;

Further, the winding order of the faces of the cube a is clockwise, so it has to be:

glFrontFace(GL_CCW);
glFrontFace(GL_CW);

Change the camera position to

glm::vec3 cameraPos(0.f, 0.f, 2.f);

and you'll get the following result:

Q: MS_MAX_CONCURRENT_REQ - VIES VAT Validation A:

The accepted answer explains the cause correctly: the limit belongs to the member state's backend and is shared by all VIES users worldwide — which is why your 15-second sleep changes nothing. What you can actually do, in order of impact:

  1. Backoff with jitter, not fixed sleeps. Fixed intervals synchronize you with every other client's fixed-interval retries. On MS_MAX_CONCURRENT_REQ wait random(30–60s), then random(60–120s), up to ~5 attempts.
  2. Run batches off-peak (CET). A daytime batch against DE competes with every checkout in Europe; the same batch at 03:00–06:00 CET sees a fraction of the errors.
  3. Dedupe + cache ~24h. Every avoided call is an avoided error.
  4. Classify MS_MAX_CONCURRENT_REQ as unknown, never invalid — park the failures and re-sweep at the end.

That gets a DE batch to a low single-digit error rate on first pass and ~zero after the sweep.

The build-vs-buy point. If VAT validation is production-critical, note what the above actually is: a retry queue, a cache with TTLs, per-country failure tracking, and monitoring — infrastructure you now own forever, for an upstream you don't control. That's the layer commercial VIES front-ends sell.

Disclosure: I'm the founder of EuroValidate — it keeps a warm cache and per-country circuit breakers in front of VIES, so a DE brownout returns the cached verdict instead of an error:

curl -H "X-API-Key: KEY" https://api.eurovalidate.com/v1/vat/DE811569869

{ "success": true,
  "data": { "status": "valid", "company_name": null },
  "meta": { "confidence": "HIGH", "source": "vies_cached", "response_time_ms": 2 } }

confidence + source tell you exactly how fresh the verdict is when Germany is down, and there's a batch endpoint (up to 1000 numbers per call) so you don't manage the concurrency at all. Free tier (100 req/mo, no card) is enough to compare error rates against your current script. Either way — jitter + off-peak + dedupe above works with plain VIES too.
